director.chapterArc: A practical debate exposes the missing anchor and turns Callie’s new power into a survival necessity. Familiar work briefly restores her competence, but spending her gate money raises the personal cost of experimentation. She can summon the Edge only by accepting its present shape; every attempt to force the Ward fails until an accidental falling crate reveals the true mechanism: not fright or raised arms, but a planted stance. The discovery is physically convincing and quietly transformative, yet the chapter closes on the unchanged external problem—the mile-long scarp still offers nowhere to anchor the tackle.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder measured, observant, and tactically exact. Let anxiety register through calculations, physical stance, and depleted resources rather than emotional display. Treat both manifestations as cold mechanics, never spectacle. The dry humor should release pressure briefly without making Ines playful or Callie’s mother broad. The final discovery is recognition, not triumph; the scarp must reclaim the last word.

cues.delivery: Make the distributed crates sound like a tactical inventory; let the final reference to her mother expose the true risk only at the landing, with no plea in it.
cues.from: "Three days on the scarp with the crates spread out up the whole length of the road. Some at the bottom, some at the top, some in the middle. Every stack a thing to guard." She made herself finish it. "And every day we're on it, my mother's on it."
cues.through: "Three days on the scarp with the crates spread out up the whole length of the road. Some at the bottom, some at the top, some in the middle. Every stack a thing to guard." She made herself finish it. "And every day we're on it, my mother's on it."
cues.reason: The logistics argument becomes personally dangerous.

cues.delivery: Give the mother’s confidence a dry, exhausted edge: she knows the problem is nearly impossible and chooses sleep over ceremony.
cues.from: "Well," said Callie's mother, from her place against the wall, "you've all got until the bottom of the hill to think of one. I've every faith in you. I'm going to sleep."
cues.through: "Well," said Callie's mother, from her place against the wall, "you've all got until the bottom of the hill to think of one. I've every faith in you. I'm going to sleep."
cues.reason: Her understated exit breaks the deadlock without dissolving its stakes.

cues.delivery: Keep the profanity itself small; the humor lies in Otto’s grave embarrassment afterward, observed without teasing him.
cues.from: Otto swore at it. It was the first time Callie had heard him swear, and he did it very quietly and went red afterward.
cues.through: Otto swore at it. It was the first time Callie had heard him swear, and he did it very quietly and went red afterward.
cues.reason: A rare ordinary human beat releases pressure.

cues.delivery: Build through disciplined accounting, not panic. Each clause closes another option until “a girl with a hook” lands as Callie’s unsentimental fear of being useless.
cues.from: "It's my gate money," said Callie. "It's what I was going to put on the table at Meridian, so they'd see we could pay. And if I drink it, it's gone. And I want to drink some of it anyway, because the scarp's tomorrow, and if I've got nothing in me at the bottom of the hill, I'm a girl with a hook. If I've got something in me, I might be more than that. I don't know what more yet. I want to find out while there's still time to find out." She looked at the tin. "And it's mine. It's in the book."
cues.through: "It's my gate money," said Callie. "It's what I was going to put on the table at Meridian, so they'd see we could pay. And if I drink it, it's gone. And I want to drink some of it anyway, because the scarp's tomorrow, and if I've got nothing in me at the bottom of the hill, I'm a girl with a hook. If I've got something in me, I might be more than that. I don't know what more yet. I want to find out while there's still time to find out." She looked at the tin. "And it's mine. It's in the book."
cues.reason: Callie states the survival gamble behind spending her future security.

cues.delivery: Protective and firm, with maternal authority carried by evidence. Keep the warmth beneath the argument; do not sentimentalize the sacrifice.
cues.from: "It's hers," said Callie's mother, from the bed. She had not been asleep either. Nobody on this wagon was ever asleep. "Pell, I've known her longer than you have. She hasn't spent one thing on herself since the spring. Not one thing. If she wants to spend it on this, she's earned the right to be wrong about it."
cues.through: "It's hers," said Callie's mother, from the bed. She had not been asleep either. Nobody on this wagon was ever asleep. "Pell, I've known her longer than you have. She hasn't spent one thing on herself since the spring. Not one thing. If she wants to spend it on this, she's earned the right to be wrong about it."
cues.reason: Her mother publicly defends Callie’s right to risk her own resources.

cues.delivery: Register alien physical wrongness rather than beauty: cold rising through the body, then a grey extension that is useful, ugly, and materially present.
cues.from: It came up through her like cold water up a pump, and into her hands, and into the steel. The hook went cold. It was the cold of the inside of a well. She opened her eyes and it was there: the long grey sweep off the end of her grandfather's forged curve, following the line the hook had always made and then simply going on with it. It was four feet of dull wrong-shaped edge the colour of nothing, lying out over the road. It was exactly as ugly as it had been on the causeway.
cues.through: It came up through her like cold water up a pump, and into her hands, and into the steel. The hook went cold. It was the cold of the inside of a well. She opened her eyes and it was there: the long grey sweep off the end of her grandfather's forged curve, following the line the hook had always made and then simply going on with it. It was four feet of dull wrong-shaped edge the colour of nothing, lying out over the road. It was exactly as ugly as it had been on the causeway.
cues.reason: The Edge manifests under deliberate control for the first time.

cues.delivery: Let the objection collapse under Callie’s own honesty; “All right” is a dry concession to an unpleasant but testable hypothesis.
cues.from: "That's not — " Callie began, and stopped, because she did not know that it wasn't. "All right."
cues.through: "That's not — " Callie began, and stopped, because she did not know that it wasn't. "All right."
cues.reason: Callie reluctantly accepts Ines’s blunt experimental logic.

cues.delivery: Absolute literalness, without mockery. Ines offers repetition as competent procedure, which supplies the deadpan humor.
cues.from: "If I'd told you, you'd not have been frightened. That was the whole experiment." Ines looked down at her without any pleasure at all. "Do you want me to do it again? I'll do it again. I'm good at it."
cues.through: "If I'd told you, you'd not have been frightened. That was the whole experiment." Ines looked down at her without any pleasure at all. "Do you want me to do it again? I'll do it again. I'm good at it."
cues.reason: The failed fright experiment resolves in Ines’s characteristically clinical wit.

cues.delivery: Keep the laugh faint and muffled, a private failure of restraint from someone too tired to join the exchange openly.
cues.from: From the bed of the wagon, very faintly, came the sound of Callie's mother laughing into a blanket.
cues.through: From the bed of the wagon, very faintly, came the sound of Callie's mother laughing into a blanket.
cues.reason: The mother’s suppressed laughter provides a brief pressure release.

cues.delivery: Pell’s verdict is dry and proportionate in tone precisely because the hill is not; leave the understatement unadorned.
cues.from: "Well," he said at last. "That's a hill."
cues.through: "Well," he said at last. "That's a hill."
cues.reason: His minimal assessment acknowledges the scarp’s absurd scale.

cues.delivery: Make the falling mass and Callie’s response spatially exact. Urgency comes from inevitability; slow enough to clarify the planted foot, dropped weight, and trained catch.
cues.from: The crate came off his hip. It came down off the tailboard straight at Callie. It was the size of a small trunk and it was full of whatever Katori would not say.
cues.through: She did not throw her arms up. There was no time and it was the wrong thing. She did what she had done a thousand times under the loading rail at Thistle Ford when a sack came off a hook, which was the one thing her grandfather had drilled into her before anything else. She dropped her weight. She put her back foot behind her and planted it and set her whole body for the catch, legs and hips and back, the way you set yourself for a thing that is going to hit you whether you like it or not.
cues.reason: The crate creates immediate bodily danger and triggers the decisive stance.

cues.delivery: Hold the impossible stillness with grave restraint. The wonder is in force finding ground beyond Callie, not in any luminous display.
cues.from: The crate stopped a finger's width off her hands.
cues.through: It hung there, for no longer than half a breath. And for that half a breath Callie felt it: the other side of the yoke, taken up. It was the weight of the world going into a wall and stopping there. It went into the plant of her back foot and down, deeper than a girl goes, and found the bottom and stayed.
cues.reason: The Ward appears and Callie finally senses the other side of the yoke.

cues.delivery: Let Otto’s concern break his syntax, but keep him quiet; the repeated apology is shock and responsibility, not hysteria.
cues.from: "Sorry," said Otto. "Sorry, sorry, my ankle — are you — "
cues.through: "Sorry," said Otto. "Sorry, sorry, my ankle — are you — "
cues.reason: Otto reacts to the near injury he caused.

cues.delivery: Unfold the memory as a mechanical proof assembling itself. Land the conclusion slowly and exactly, with recognition rather than triumph.
cues.from: Callie was still on one knee on the gravel. She looked down at her own feet. Her back foot was still planted behind her, heel down, toes dug into the gravel, the way it had been planted in the silt step at the mouth of the culvert on the first night. It was the way it had been planted on the deck of the causeway when the wagon came off the rail stub and came down onto her shoulder.
cues.through: "It's not the fright," she said slowly. "And it's not my arms. It's my feet."
cues.reason: Callie connects three incidents and identifies the planted feet as the trigger.

cues.delivery: Dry inherited affection: the grandfather’s practical rebuke carries pride underneath, but the mother does not soften it.
cues.from: From up on the wagon bed, where she had been lying under a blanket with her eyes shut, Callie's mother said: "Your grandfather used to say you could stand a sack of meal on your back foot all day, if you'd only stop arguing with it."
cues.through: From up on the wagon bed, where she had been lying under a blanket with her eyes shut, Callie's mother said: "Your grandfather used to say you could stand a sack of meal on your back foot all day, if you'd only stop arguing with it."
cues.reason: The family saying confirms the discovery while restoring human warmth.

cues.delivery: Quiet certainty, with the remembered grandfather present only in the slight weight of the final word; no grief display.
cues.reason: Callie acknowledges the lesson as remembered inheritance.
